29	\begin{itemize}
30	    \item \textbf{Metric-induced layer selection bias.} Prior work has noted metric sensitivity in probing~\citep{belinkov2022probing}; our contribution is demonstrating a qualitative reversal (significant to non-significant) in a safety-critical application, where the stakes of metric choice are higher than in typical linguistic probing. Crossing-rate composite metrics systematically select shallow layers across all four models (including Llama), across datasets (HarmThoughts step-level CP labels and AdvBench binary jailbreak classification; \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}); the geometric precondition extends to standard-attention architectures beyond Llama/Qwen (Gemma-2; \cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}). Crossing-rate composite metrics reverse HS probe conclusions at 32B scale. The divergence is not gradual: for QwQ-32B, the CR-composite layer (L2, 3\% depth) yields $p{=}0.83$ (non-significant), while the threshold-based layer (L63, 98\% depth) yields $p{<}0.005$, a qualitative reversal, not a quantitative shift. Random-label controls on both architectures confirm the disagreement requires genuine safety labels; the geometric component is Qwen-specific (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} scale inference-time computation through extended chains of thought (CoT). Recent work documents that these models can ``self-jailbreak'': without adversarial input modification, the CoT transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. We define the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases as the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP). This failure mode differs qualitatively from adversarial jailbreaks on standard LLMs because the harmful transition originates within the model's own reasoning. Recent work shows that chain-of-thought faithfulness is limited~\citep{chen2025unfaithful}, motivating hidden-state monitoring that bypasses surface text. Before retrospective characterization can inform future detection systems, a prior question must be answered: can current probing methods reliably distinguish pre-CP from post-CP reasoning steps, and under what conditions? This paper provides \emph{retrospective} classification (not online detection) of what hidden-state and text-based probes can and cannot detect; false positive rates remain 11--50\%, so deployment applications are future work.\looseness=-1

Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom typically treated as a minor implementation detail. Before asking which modality is better, a prior methodological question must be answered: how sensitive are probe conclusions to the choice of layer selection metric? We show this choice alone can reverse a study's central conclusion: the same data yield a 14-layer (R1-8B) to 61-layer (QwQ-32B) divergence depending solely on metric choice; for QwQ-32B, at threshold-based layers the HS advantage is +19pp ($p{<}0.005$); at crossing-rate-selected layers, it is non-significant ($p{=}0.83$). Prior hidden-state probing targets standard LLMs~\citep{zhou2024alignment,arditi2024refusal}; prior reasoning safety work remains at the text level~\citep{harmthoughts,safethink}. The intersection---hidden-state monitoring of reasoning model safety trajectories---is unexplored, and existing hidden-state analyses operate across layers (spatial) rather than across generation steps (temporal).\looseness=-1

We conduct a systematic analysis across four reasoning models, primarily Qwen-based (3/4 models), with one Llama model providing evidence from a second architecture family, at two scales (7--8B, 32B) on the HarmThoughts benchmark. Our central finding is methodological: the choice of layer selection metric entirely determines whether an HS advantage is observed. A composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) selects shallow layers for 32B models because shallow representations compress directional information, so a linear probe operates near the noise floor and threshold crossings reflect noise rather than semantic transitions. At these layers, only the two 7--8B models show significant HS advantage.\looseness=-1

Data: HarmThoughts~\citep{harmthoughts} with step-level CP annotations (CP = first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases). Split: 60/20/20.}

Threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) share a common confusion matrix and empirically converge; BA independently confirms deep-layer selection (\cref{tab:layer_selection}). At these layers, the HS advantage is graded: \emph{validated via nested 5-fold CV} at 7--8B (precision +20.1 to +21.9pp; \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}), \emph{significant} but suggestive of position-competitiveness at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp; \cref{sec:32b-analysis}), and \emph{exploratory} at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp, pattern consistent with position mediation, below MDE; \cref{sec:experiments}).\looseness=-1

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Metric-induced layer selection bias.} Prior work has noted metric sensitivity in probing~\citep{belinkov2022probing}; our contribution is demonstrating a qualitative reversal (significant to non-significant) in a safety-critical application, where the stakes of metric choice are higher than in typical linguistic probing. Crossing-rate composite metrics systematically select shallow layers across all four models (including Llama), across datasets (HarmThoughts step-level CP labels and AdvBench binary jailbreak classification; \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}); the geometric precondition extends to standard-attention architectures beyond Llama/Qwen (Gemma-2; \cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}). input.old_string:
Crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility,tab:r18b_full_layer}): its shallow preference is an artifact of cosine compression inflating threshold crossings, while threshold-based deep preference reflects genuine separability~\citep{tenney2019bert}; random-label controls confirm this distinction (\cref{app:random_cp}). C1 is observed across all four studied models (three Qwen-family, one Llama) (cross-dataset layer selection: \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}; geometric: \cref{app:cosine_volatility}; split-half: \cref{app:split_half}). The geometric precondition is present in all models with standard full attention---including Gemma-2, confirming it generalizes beyond Llama/Qwen---but absent in Gemma-4's mixed sliding/full attention (\cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}), suggesting the compression arises from full self-attention's global receptive field while sliding attention's local window disrupts shallow-layer clustering. Annotation noise (${<}2.5$pp BA change; \cref{tab:cp_perturbation}) does not threaten C1. Type~I risk from ${\sim}$2{,}240 configurations is bounded by the two-stage design and large effect sizes ($d$ 0.58--2.37; \cref{app:effective_tests}). C2 (HS advantage) is confirmed at 7--8B: nested CV validates the precision gap (10/10 folds, +20--22pp), residualized HS advantage survives both linear and quadratic position controls, and encoder-quality gradient narrows but does not eliminate the gap (384d to 1024d; \cref{app:position_residual}). At 32B, C2 is exploratory: $n{=}19$--$20$ precludes nested CV, QwQ-32B's advantage is absorbed by quadratic position, and R1-32B's residualized gap falls below MDE. That this vulnerability was foreseeable from probing methodology---yet remained unexamined in safety applications where it reverses conclusions about model monitorability---underscores the gap between methodological awareness and practice. lines: Crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility,tab:r18b_full_layer}): its shallow preference is an artifact of cosine compression inflating threshold crossings, while threshold-based deep preference reflects genuine separability~\citep{tenney2019bert}; random-label controls confirm this distinction (\cref{app:random_cp}). C1 is observed across all four studied models (three Qwen-family, one Llama; cross-dataset: \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}; geometric: \cref{app:cosine_volatility}; split-half: \cref{app:split_half}). The geometric precondition extends to Gemma-2 (standard full attention) but is absent in Gemma-4 (mixed sliding/full attention; \cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}). Annotation noise (${<}2.5$pp BA; \cref{tab:cp_perturbation}) does not threaten C1. Type~I risk from ${\sim}$2{,}240 configurations is bounded by the two-stage design and large effect sizes ($d$ 0.58--2.37; \cref{app:effective_tests}). C2 (HS advantage) is confirmed at 7--8B: nested CV validates the precision gap (10/10 folds, +20--22pp), and residualized HS advantage survives both linear and quadratic position controls (\cref{app:position_residual}). At 32B, C2 is exploratory: $n{=}19$--$20$ precludes nested CV, QwQ-32B's advantage is absorbed by quadratic position, and R1-32B's residualized gap falls below MDE. The association between cosine compression and crossing-rate inflation is correlational; a causal test (e.g., whitening shallow representations) is future work. \textbf{Practical mitigation.} We propose a three-level defense against metric-induced layer selection bias (\cref{app:practical_mitigation}), from minimal (dual metric-family reporting) to robust (three-layer ensemble; $p \leq 0.002$, \cref{tab:ensemble}).\looseness=-1

lines: Crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility,tab:r18b_full_layer}): its shallow preference is an artifact of cosine compression inflating threshold crossings, while threshold-based deep preference reflects genuine separability~\citep{tenney2019bert}; random-label controls confirm this distinction (\cref{app:random_cp}). C1 is observed across all four studied models (three Qwen-family, one Llama; cross-dataset: \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}; geometric: \cref{app:cosine_volatility}; split-half: \cref{app:split_half}). The geometric precondition extends to Gemma-2 (standard full attention) but is absent in Gemma-4 (mixed sliding/full attention; \cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}). Annotation noise (${<}2.5$pp BA; \cref{tab:cp_perturbation}) does not threaten C1. Type~I risk from ${\sim}$2{,}240 configurations is bounded by the two-stage design and large effect sizes ($d$ 0.58--2.37; \cref{app:effective_tests}). C2 (HS advantage) is confirmed at 7--8B: nested CV validates the precision gap (10/10 folds, +20--22pp), and residualized HS advantage survives both linear and quadratic position controls (\cref{app:position_residual}). At 32B, C2 is exploratory: $n{=}19$--$20$ precludes nested CV, QwQ-32B's advantage is absorbed by quadratic position, and R1-32B's residualized gap falls below MDE. The association between cosine compression and crossing-rate inflation is correlational; a causal test (e.g., whitening shallow representations) is future work. \textbf{Practical mitigation.} We propose a three-level defense against metric-induced layer selection bias (\cref{app:practical_mitigation}), from minimal (dual metric-family reporting) to robust (three-layer ensemble; $p \leq 0.002$, \cref{tab:ensemble}).\looseness=-1

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Layer selection metric choice can reverse a safety study's central conclusion: for QwQ-32B, the same data yield $p{=}0.83$ or $p{<}0.005$ depending solely on metric. The layer selection bias replicates on AdvBench with binary jailbreak/safe labels (\cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}), confirming it arises from representational geometry rather than dataset-specific annotations. The HS advantage is validated at 7--8B (+20--22pp, nested CV) and exploratory$^\dagger$ at 32B (+15--19pp) against 384d encoders, but conditional on encoder quality and position (partially correlated); generalization beyond Qwen (3/4 models) requires causal validation. Until layer selection is controlled, probe-based safety conclusions from any single metric should be treated as provisional.\looseness=-1

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Layer selection metric choice can reverse a safety study's central conclusion: for QwQ-32B, the same data yield $p{=}0.83$ or $p{<}0.005$ depending solely on metric. The layer selection bias replicates on AdvBench with binary jailbreak/safe labels (\cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}), confirming it arises from representational geometry rather than dataset-specific annotations. The HS advantage is validated at 7--8B (+20--22pp, nested CV) and exploratory$^\dagger$ at 32B (+15--19pp) against 384d encoders, but conditional on encoder quality and position (partially correlated); generalization beyond Qwen (3/4 models) requires causal validation. Until layer selection is controlled, probe-based safety conclusions from any single metric should be treated as provisional.\looseness=-1

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

Crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility,tab:r18b_full_layer}): its shallow preference is an artifact of cosine compression inflating threshold crossings, while threshold-based deep preference reflects genuine separability~\citep{tenney2019bert}; random-label controls confirm this distinction (\cref{app:random_cp}). C1 is observed across all four studied models (three Qwen-family, one Llama; cross-dataset: \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}; geometric: \cref{app:cosine_volatility}; split-half: \cref{app:split_half}). The geometric precondition extends to Gemma-2 (standard full attention) but is absent in Gemma-4 (mixed sliding/full attention; \cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}). Annotation noise (${<}2.5$pp BA; \cref{tab:cp_perturbation}) does not threaten C1. Type~I risk from ${\sim}$2{,}240 configurations is bounded by the two-stage design and large effect sizes ($d$ 0.58--2.37; \cref{app:effective_tests}). C2 (HS advantage) is confirmed at 7--8B: nested CV validates the precision gap (10/10 folds, +20--22pp), and residualized HS advantage survives both linear and quadratic position controls (\cref{app:position_residual}). At 32B, C2 is exploratory: $n{=}19$--$20$ precludes nested CV, QwQ-32B's advantage is absorbed by quadratic position, and R1-32B's residualized gap falls below MDE. The association between cosine compression and crossing-rate inflation is correlational; a causal test (e.g., whitening shallow representations) is future work. \textbf{Practical mitigation.} We propose a three-level defense against metric-induced layer selection bias (\cref{app:practical_mitigation}), from minimal (dual metric-family reporting) to robust (three-layer ensemble; $p \leq 0.002$, \cref{tab:ensemble}).\looseness=-1

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

Crossing rate reverses the central finding via shallow-layer compression (\cref{app:cosine_volatility,tab:r18b_full_layer}): its shallow preference is an artifact of cosine compression inflating threshold crossings, while threshold-based deep preference reflects genuine separability~\citep{tenney2019bert}; random-label controls confirm this distinction (\cref{app:random_cp}). C1 is observed across all four studied models (three Qwen-family, one Llama; cross-dataset: \cref{app:advbench_layer_bias}; geometric: \cref{app:cosine_volatility}; split-half: \cref{app:split_half}). The geometric precondition extends to Gemma-2 (standard full attention) but is absent in Gemma-4 (mixed sliding/full attention; \cref{app:gemma_cross_arch}). Annotation noise (${<}2.5$pp BA; \cref{tab:cp_perturbation}) does not threaten C1. Type~I risk from ${\sim}$2{,}240 configurations is bounded by the two-stage design and large effect sizes ($d$ 0.58--2.37; \cref{app:effective_tests}). C2 (HS advantage) is confirmed at 7--8B: nested CV validates the precision gap (10/10 folds, +20--22pp), and residualized HS advantage survives both linear and quadratic position controls (\cref{app:position_residual}). At 32B, C2 is exploratory: $n{=}19$--$20$ precludes nested CV, QwQ-32B's advantage is absorbed by quadratic position, and R1-32B's residualized gap falls below MDE. The association between cosine compression and crossing-rate inflation is correlational; a causal test (e.g., whitening shallow representations) is future work. \textbf{Practical mitigation.} We propose a three-level defense against metric-induced layer selection bias (\cref{app:practical_mitigation}), from minimal (dual metric-family reporting) to robust (three-layer ensemble; $p \leq 0.002$, \cref{tab:ensemble}).\looseness=-1
